query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the chromium content in the alloy composition enhances oxidation resistance by promoting the formation of a protective chromium oxide scale.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (e.g., HESA) initially formulated with lower Cr content alongside elements such as Ni, Co, Fe, Al, Ti, Nb, minor C, Mo, and W.
generation.intervention: Increase the Cr content in the alloy during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature oxidizing environments (such as elevated temperature air or molten salt conditions) where oxidation is a concern.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 (chromium oxide) scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Chromium present in the alloy reacts with oxygen during high-temperature exposure to form a stable, protective chromia barrier that slows further oxidation and limits corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy with increased Cr content is expected to show a reduced oxidation rate (lower mass loss and slower oxide scale growth) compared to the same alloy with lower Cr content.
generation.baseline: The performance of the alloy with the standard, lower Cr content under identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected to be significant in high-temperature exposures but may depend on the overall alloy composition and interactions with other elements, especially in complex HEAs or RHEAs.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the oxidation resistance improvement is uncertain and may vary with the alloy’s full composition, processing conditions, and specific testing environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one with the standard (baseline) Cr content and one with elevated Cr content. Subject both sets to high-temperature oxidizing conditions (e.g., exposure to air at 1000°C or exposure to molten salt environments) for a fixed time period.
measurements: Mass change (mass loss or gain) measurements over time.
Oxide scale characterization using SEM/EDS to measure thickness and adherence.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to confirm the formation of Cr2O3 on the surface.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with increased Cr content does not show statistically significant lower mass loss, slower oxide scale growth, or more uniform and protective Cr2O3 layer formation compared to the baseline alloy under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
